lessons.title: Determining Optimal Harvest Time
lessons.body:
Cassava roots can be harvested from 6 to 24 months after planting, depending on variety and purpose. For starch extraction, you want maximum starch content, which usually peaks between 9 and 12 months for most African varieties. Harvest too early (before 8 months) and roots are small with low starch; too late (after 18 months) and starch turns to sugar, roots become woody, and post-harvest deterioration speeds up. So the sweet spot is 9â12 months for starch.

How do you know it's time? First, check the leaves: when lower leaves turn yellow and drop, and the plant stops growing new leaves, it's a sign. Second, look at the roots: dig up one or two sample plants. Mature roots have a thick, dark brown skin that is easy to peel, and the flesh is white and firm. If the skin is thin and pale, they are still young. Third, do a simple starch test: grate a small piece of root, squeeze the juice onto a clear glass, and let it settle. If a thick white layer of starch forms at the bottom within 30 minutes, starch content is high.

In Africa, many farmers harvest at 12 months for maximum yield, but if you want early cash, you can harvest at 8â9 months. However, for starch extraction, waiting until 10â12 months gives you more starch per root. Also consider the dry season: harvesting in dry weather reduces root rot and makes peeling easier. If you harvest in the rainy season, roots absorb water, starch gets diluted, and roots rot faster.

Tools for checking: a machete or hoe to dig, a knife to cut the root, a clear glass or jar for the starch test, and a scale to weigh sample roots. Record the date you planted and the date you harvest. Keep notes on starch yield per root. Over time, you'll learn the best time for your variety and soil.

Remember: once roots mature, they don't store well in the ground. If you leave them too long, they become fibrous and lose starch. So plan your harvest when you have labour and a processing facility ready.

lessons.title: Harvesting Techniques for Cassava Roots
lessons.body:
Harvesting cassava is hard work, but with the right technique you can avoid damaging roots and reduce losses. The goal is to lift the roots out of the soil without breaking or bruising them, because damaged roots rot quickly and lose starch.

Start by cutting the stems about 30â40 cm above the ground using a sharp machete or cutlass. This gives you a handle to pull the plant. Then, use a strong hoe or a digging fork to loosen the soil around the roots. Insert the tool about 30 cm away from the stem and push down, then lever the soil up. Do not dig directly into the root clusterâyou will cut roots. Once the soil is loose, grab the stem and pull firmly. If the plant resists, loosen more soil. The whole root cluster should come out. If some roots break off, dig them out separately.

For large fields, you can use a tractor-drawn cassava lifter, but most smallholders in Africa harvest by hand. A team of 2â3 people can harvest about 200â300 kg of fresh roots per day. Work in the cool hours of the morning or late afternoon to avoid heat stress. Wear gloves to protect your hands from the rough stems and soil.

After lifting, shake off excess soil gently. Do not bang roots against each other or drop them. Cut the roots from the stem with a sharp knife, leaving about 2â3 cm of the root attached to the stem. Then, trim off any damaged or rotten parts. Place roots in a shaded area on a clean tarpaulin or mat. Do not leave them in the sunâsunlight causes greening and increases deterioration.

If you are harvesting for starch, process within 24â48 hours. The sooner, the better. If you must wait, keep roots in a cool, shaded, ventilated place. Never pile roots in a heapâthey heat up and rot. Spread them in a single layer. Use baskets or crates for transport to avoid bruising. With careful harvesting, you can reduce post-harvest losses from 30% to under 10%.

lessons.title: Sorting and Grading Cassava Roots
lessons.body:
Sorting and grading are simple steps that make a big difference in starch quality and price. After harvesting, spread your roots on a clean surface under shade. Look at each root and separate them into three groups: Grade A, Grade B, and rejects.

Grade A roots are fresh, firm, and undamaged. They have no cuts, bruises, or soft spots. The skin is intact and the root is straight or slightly curved. These roots give the highest starch yield and are best for processing. Grade B roots have minor damageâsmall cuts, slight bruising, or irregular shapeâbut are still firm and not rotting. They can be processed quickly or sold for fresh consumption. Rejects are roots that are soft, rotten, infested by insects, or have a bad smell. These must be discarded immediately because they will spoil the whole batch and reduce starch quality.

How to sort: work on a table or mat. Use a sharp knife to trim off any damaged parts. If a root is partially rotten, cut away the rotten part and check the rest. If more than 20% is rotten, discard the whole root. For starch extraction, you want clean, healthy roots. Even a small amount of rot can introduce bacteria that ferment the starch and cause off-flavours.

Grading also considers size. Large, thick roots (more than 5 cm diameter) are easier to peel and grate. Small, thin roots are more work and have less starch. You can sell Grade A roots to starch factories or process them yourself. Grade B can be used for home consumption or local markets. Rejects can be composted or fed to animals after proper treatment (but never use rotten roots for starch).

Sorting should be done within 12 hours of harvest. Keep the groups separate in different baskets or piles. Label them if you are selling. A simple grading system like this helps you get a better price and ensures your starch is clean. In many African markets, ungraded roots fetch 20â30% less than graded roots. So take the time to sort.

lessons.title: Transportation and Storage of Fresh Roots
lessons.body:
Fresh cassava roots are perishable. They start to deteriorate within 24â48 hours after harvest. So transportation and storage must be quick and careful. The goal is to keep roots cool, shaded, and ventilated to slow down spoilage.

For transportation, use clean baskets, crates, or sacks. Never use airtight plastic bagsâthey trap heat and moisture, causing rot. If you use sacks, make sure they are woven and breathable. Load roots gently; do not throw or drop them. Stack baskets no more than three high to avoid crushing the bottom layer. If you are transporting by truck or pickup, cover the load with a tarpaulin to protect from sun and rain, but leave the sides open for air. Travel during the cooler parts of the day (early morning or evening). The maximum transport time should be 6â8 hours. If you must travel longer, keep roots in a cool, shaded place overnight.

For storage, fresh roots can be stored for a short time using simple methods. The most common in Africa is to spread roots in a thin layer (one or two roots deep) on a raised platform or on the floor of a well-ventilated shed. Keep them out of direct sunlight. Sprinkle water lightly on the floor to keep humidity high (80â90%) but not wet. This can keep roots fresh for 3â5 days. Another method is to store roots in trenches: dig a shallow trench 30 cm deep in a shaded area, line it with leaves, place roots in a single layer, cover with leaves and soil. This can extend storage to 1â2 weeks. However, for starch extraction, you should process within 48 hours. Longer storage increases starch loss and off-flavours.

Do not store roots in piles. Piles generate heat and rot. Also, never store roots near chemicals or fuelâthey absorb odours. If you see signs of mould or soft spots, remove those roots immediately. For commercial starch production, plan your harvest and processing so that roots go from farm to grater within 24 hours. That is the best way to preserve starch quality.

lessons.title: Post-Harvest Physiological Deterioration
lessons.body:
Post-harvest physiological deterioration (PPD) is the natural process that makes fresh cassava roots go bad within 1â3 days after harvest. It starts as blue-black streaks inside the root, then the root becomes soft, brown, and rotten. PPD is not caused by insects or microbes initiallyâit is a wound response by the root itself. When you cut or damage the root during harvest, enzymes react with oxygen and cause discoloration. This reduces starch quality and yield.

Why does PPD matter for starch extraction? Because deteriorated roots have lower starch content, the starch is darker, and it may have off-flavours. A root with 25% starch can drop to 15% within 48 hours. That means you lose 40% of your starch. So preventing PPD is critical.

How to slow PPD: First, minimize damage during harvest. Use careful digging and handling. Second, keep roots cool. PPD speeds up in heat. Store roots in shade or in a cool room. Third, process quickly. The best way is to grate roots within 24 hours. If you cannot process immediately, you can use simple treatments. For example, dipping roots in a solution of 1% sodium metabisulfite (food-grade) for 5 minutes can delay PPD for up to 5 days. But this chemical may not be available everywhere. Another method is to store roots in moist sawdust or leaves, which reduces oxygen and slows the reaction. Some farmers in Nigeria and Ghana store roots in trenches with moist soil, which keeps them fresh for up to 2 weeks.

However, for starch extraction, the safest approach is to process within 24 hours. If you must wait, keep roots in a single layer in a well-ventilated, shaded area. Do not pile them. Check for signs of PPD: cut a root openâif you see blue-black streaks, it has started. Use those roots first. If roots are already soft and smelly, discard them. Remember, PPD is irreversible. Once it starts, you cannot stop it. So speed is your best tool.

lessons.title: Pre-Processing Steps: Washing and Peeling
lessons.body:
Before you can extract starch, you must wash and peel the cassava roots. These steps remove dirt, sand, and the outer skin, which contains bitter compounds and reduces starch purity. Clean roots give you white, high-quality starch. Dirty roots give you brown, gritty starch that sells for less.

Washing: Start by soaking roots in a large basin or drum of clean water for 10â15 minutes. This softens the dirt. Then, scrub each root with a stiff brush or a piece of rough cloth. Use a brush with plastic bristlesânot metal, which can scratch the root. For large quantities, you can build a simple washing trough: a slanted wooden or concrete trough with water flowing through it. Put roots at the top, and as they roll down, they rub against each other and the sides, removing dirt. Rinse with clean water. Change the water oftenâif it gets muddy, you are just spreading dirt. For 100 kg of roots, you need about 200 litres of clean water. After washing, roots should look clean and the skin should be visible.

Peeling: You can peel cassava with a sharp knife or a traditional peeler. The skin has two layers: a thin outer layer (brown) and a thicker inner layer (pinkish or white). For starch, you should remove both layers because the inner layer contains cyanogenic glucosides (bitter compounds) that can affect starch quality. Use a knife to cut off the ends, then slit the skin lengthwise and peel it off. Work on a clean surface. For 100 kg of roots, peeling takes about 2â3 hours with 2 people. Wear gloves if your hands are sensitive. The peels can be composted or fed to animals after drying (but not fresh, as they contain cyanide).

After peeling, cut the roots into small pieces (about 2â3 cm) to make grating easier. Then, wash the peeled roots again in clean water to remove any remaining dirt or starch. Now they are ready for grating. Remember: wash and peel within 24 hours of harvest to avoid PPD. If you peel too early, the roots darken. So time your processing: harvest, wash, peel, grateâall in one day for best starch yield.

quiz.q: What is the optimal harvest age for cassava roots intended for starch extraction?
quiz.explanation: Starch content peaks between 9 and 12 months for most African varieties.

quiz.q: Which sign indicates that cassava roots are mature and ready for harvest?
options: A) Leaves are all green and new shoots appear
B) Lower leaves turn yellow and drop
C) Roots are thin and pale
D) Stems are still soft and green
quiz.explanation: When lower leaves yellow and drop, the plant has stopped growing and roots are mature.

quiz.q: What simple test can you do to check starch content in cassava roots?
options: B) Squeeze juice onto a glass and look for white sediment
D) Count the number of leaves
quiz.explanation: Starch settles as a white layer at the bottom of the glass within 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Why is harvesting in the dry season preferred for starch extraction?
options: A) Roots are easier to peel and rot less
C) Starch turns to sugar faster
quiz.explanation: Dry weather reduces root rot and makes peeling easier, preserving starch quality.

quiz.q: What should you do first when harvesting cassava?
options: B) Cut the stems 30-40 cm above ground
C) Dig into the root cluster
quiz.explanation: Cutting stems first gives a handle to pull the plant without damaging roots.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for loosening soil around cassava roots?
options: B) A hoe or digging fork
quiz.explanation: A hoe or digging fork lifts soil without cutting the roots.

quiz.q: How soon should cassava roots be processed after harvest for best starch quality?
quiz.explanation: Processing within 24-48 hours minimizes starch loss and deterioration.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a Grade A cassava root?
options: B) Firm, undamaged, with intact skin
quiz.explanation: Grade A roots are fresh, firm, and free from damage.

quiz.q: What should you do with rejected cassava roots?
options: A) Mix them with good roots
quiz.explanation: Rejects can spoil the whole batch and reduce starch quality, so they must be discarded.

quiz.q: Why is it important to sort cassava roots before processing?
options: A) To increase starch yield and quality
quiz.explanation: Sorting removes damaged and rotten roots, ensuring clean, high-quality starch.

quiz.q: What is the best way to transport fresh cassava roots?
options: B) In woven baskets or crates
C) In a pile on a truck bed
quiz.explanation: Woven baskets or crates allow ventilation and reduce bruising.

quiz.q: How long can fresh cassava roots be stored in a well-ventilated shed?
quiz.explanation: With proper ventilation and humidity, roots can stay fresh for 3-5 days.

quiz.q: What is a trench storage method for cassava roots?
options: B) Burying roots in a shallow trench with leaves and soil
quiz.explanation: Trench storage keeps roots cool and moist, extending shelf life to 1-2 weeks.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid piling cassava roots during storage?
options: A) Piles generate heat and cause rot
C) Piles make roots too dry
quiz.explanation: Piles trap heat and moisture, leading to rapid deterioration.

quiz.q: What causes post-harvest physiological deterioration (PPD) in cassava?
options: B) Wound response by the root itself
quiz.explanation: PPD is a natural wound response involving enzymes and oxygen.

quiz.q: What are the first visible signs of PPD in cassava roots?
options: B) Blue-black streaks inside the root
C) Green spots on the skin
quiz.explanation: PPD starts as blue-black discoloration inside the root.

quiz.q: How much starch can be lost within 48 hours due to PPD?
quiz.explanation: Starch content can drop from 25% to 15%, a 40% loss, within 48 hours.

quiz.q: Which treatment can delay PPD in cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Sodium metabisulfite is a food-grade chemical that slows PPD for up to 5 days.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prevent PPD for starch extraction?
options: A) Store roots in a pile
C) Leave roots in the sun
D) Wash roots and store wet
quiz.explanation: Processing quickly is the most effective way to avoid PPD and preserve starch.

quiz.q: Why should you remove both the outer and inner skin of cassava roots for starch?
options: A) To reduce bitterness and improve starch purity
quiz.explanation: The inner skin contains cyanogenic glucosides that affect starch quality.

quiz.q: How long should you soak cassava roots before scrubbing?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for 10-15 minutes softens dirt for easier scrubbing.

quiz.q: What type of brush is recommended for washing cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Plastic bristles are stiff enough to remove dirt without scratching the root.

quiz.q: How much clean water is needed to wash 100 kg of cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: About 200 litres of clean water is required for 100 kg of roots.

quiz.q: What should you do with cassava peels after peeling?
options: A) Compost or dry for animal feed
B) Use directly as fresh animal feed
quiz.explanation: Peels contain cyanide and must be dried or composted before use.

quiz.q: Why should you cut peeled cassava roots into small pieces before grating?
options: A) To make grating easier and faster
quiz.explanation: Small pieces are easier to feed into a grater and improve extraction efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time you should wait between harvesting and washing/peeling?
quiz.explanation: Washing and peeling should be done within 24 hours to avoid PPD and darkening.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of a mature cassava root?
quiz.explanation: Thin, pale skin indicates an immature root.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using a tractor-drawn cassava lifter?
options: A) It reduces labour and speeds up harvesting
quiz.explanation: Mechanical lifters harvest large fields faster with less manual labour.

quiz.q: How should you store cassava roots if you cannot process them immediately?
options: A) In a single layer in a cool, shaded, ventilated area
B) In a large pile under the sun
quiz.explanation: A single layer in shade allows air circulation and slows deterioration.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of sodium metabisulfite solution for delaying PPD?
quiz.explanation: A 1% solution dipped for 5 minutes can delay PPD for up to 5 days.
